title: North Korea-Linked Hackers Turn Web Servers Into Stealthy Espionage Backdoors
content_md: The campaign targeted organizations in South Korea’s automotive and media sectors, using compromised edge servers to steal credentials, monitor victims, inject malicious content into web traffic, and maintain long-term access. At the center of the operation is a modified HAProxy load balancer, named the “ted backdoor.” Rather than deploying a separate and easily detectable web shell, the attackers compiled the implant directly into HAProxy version 2.8.12. This lets the malware use HAProxy’s native filtering system, memory pools, event scheduler, and process controls while the server continues handling legitimate traffic normally. Rapid7 assesses the activity may be linked to North Korean threat actors with medium confidence. The targeting of South Korean organizations, use of simple XOR encryption and substitution ciphers, and command-and-control domains previously associated with APT37 support the assessment. However, the initial access method and a definitive attribution remain unconfirmed. North Korean Webserver Backdoors The ted backdoor can intercept decrypted HTTP traffic inside HAProxy before it reaches the backend server. It can inspect selected requests, capture session cookies and HTTP headers, and identify high-value targets based on IP addresses, URLs, referrers, and user-agent strings.
